pages.title: What has been observed
pages.instruction: Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Fictional city data note · simulated source
pages.subject: Three months of trips
paragraphs: The teaching dataset records average daily trips of 100 in January, 120 in February and 140 in March. These are simulated figures, not news or a statistical study. The series shows a rise across three observations, but provides no earlier years, seasonal pattern or explanation of who is travelling.

A projection continuing the same increase would be conditional on similar circumstances. It should not be relabelled as an observed April result. A recommendation can acknowledge a possible pressure on services without claiming that these figures alone establish a permanent rate, a single cause or an inevitable worst-case outcome.

pages.title: What the plan assumes
pages.instruction: Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Transport scenario · simulated source
pages.subject: Capacity must match the need
paragraphs: The scenario includes additional transport starting next month. The headline capacity estimate treats the extra service as if it covers the demand under discussion. The record confirms a service plan but leaves the detailed time coverage for a later check. A group member therefore suggests that no further action will be necessary.

That conclusion depends on more than a total number. Capacity at the wrong time or place may not meet the actual need. The task is to identify which assumption should be tested and what information would change the recommendation. Monitoring can be a sensible action if it has a focus, an owner and a clear trigger for reviewing the plan.

lines.audioText: What would be a more defensible claim?

lines.text: We were going to recommend no further action because the extra service looked sufficient

pages.title: Forecast without overstating
pages.instruction: Explain your prediction and say what could make it wrong

pages.title: Total capacity is not all-day coverage
pages.instruction: Listen for the new information and decide how to respond
pages.message: Hi, Ana. There’s a limitation in the transport projection. The extra service is confirmed, but it only runs in the morning peak. The demand we’re discussing includes afternoon trips as well. So the added total capacity cannot automatically be treated as coverage for every part of the day. That doesn’t prove demand will keep rising at the same rate, or that the whole plan will fail. It does mean we should qualify the assumption that the extra service removes the problem. Could you revise the recommendation with that distinction? A useful next step would identify what afternoon information is needed and what observation would trigger another decision, rather than simply moving from “everything is solved” to “it’s bound to get worse”
